checkpoints.title: Tradeoff duel
checkpoints.prompt: A query filters by tenant_id, then a created_at range, and returns newest rows first. Which index best matches it?

options.label: Two separate single-column indexes
options.verdict: The planner may combine separate indexes, but it still has more work and may need an explicit sort. The indexes do not encode the query's equality-then-range access pattern together.

options.label: Composite (tenant_id, created_at DESC)
options.sub: match equality first and ordered range second
options.verdict: The leftmost tenant equality narrows the index, and the following timestamp entries are already ordered for the range and result ordering. The tradeoff is added write and storage cost.

defend.prompt: Which claims correctly qualify the composite index?

options.label: Column order must reflect actual predicates and sorting
Every insert and update may pay index-maintenance cost
INCLUDE columns can enable an index-only plan
The index guarantees every possible tenant query is fast

defend.explain: Indexes are workload-specific. A covering form can avoid heap access for a narrow projection, but wider indexes consume memory and increase write amplification. Verify the real plan with EXPLAIN ANALYZE instead of assuming the optimizer will use it.

checkpoints.title: Index reasoning ladder
checkpoints.prompt: Reason from index structure and access patterns.

rungs.q: Which index is the default fit for equality, ranges, and ordered scans?
rungs.note: B-trees preserve key order while supporting efficient point and range lookups.

rungs.q: For an index on (tenant_id, created_at), which predicate can use its leftmost prefix directly?
rungs.note: The index is ordered first by tenant_id; skipping that leading column generally prevents a direct prefix lookup.

rungs.q: Which index is designed to map terms to matching documents?
rungs.note: An inverted index stores a posting list for each token and powers full-text retrieval.

checkpoints.explain: Choose the structure from the operation: B-trees for ordered keys, inverted indexes for text terms, and geospatial structures for spatial neighborhoods. Then choose composite order from the workload's predicates.

checkpoints.title: Architecture builder
checkpoints.prompt: Build the path of a covered composite-index query.
checkpoints.explain: The planner selects the composite index, traverses its B-tree to the matching prefix and range, and reads the projected values from the index itself. When visibility rules permit an index-only scan, included columns avoid random heap fetches and the index order avoids a separate sort.

checkpoints.title: Spot the bottleneck
checkpoints.prompt: A formerly fast write-heavy table slows after months of tuning. Which signal identifies the bottleneck?
checkpoints.explain: Every inserted or changed row must maintain applicable indexes. Twelve unused indexes add write amplification, WAL volume, storage, and cache pressure without serving reads. Confirm usage statistics and remove redundant indexes through the database's safe operational process.

wrong.Buffer Hit Rate: A high, healthy hit rate does not explain the write regression and suggests reads are mostly memory-resident.
wrong.Read QPS: Read traffic is flat, so it does not correlate with the worsening write path.
wrong.Lock Waits: Low, steady lock waits do not match the accumulated per-write index maintenance cost.
